`SequenceMatcher` builds its matching blocks by divide and conquer around the longest contiguous match. `get_matching_blocks` starts with the whole of `a` and `b`, asks `find_longest_match` for the single longest block where `a[i:i+k] == b[j:j+k]`, records it, and then repeats the same search on the region to the left of that block and the region to the right (using an explicit queue rather than recursion). Because each sub-search is confined to the pieces strictly left or strictly right of an already chosen block, the blocks can never cross. At the end they are sorted, adjacent blocks are merged, and a `(len(a), len(b), 0)` sentinel is appended. `get_opcodes` and `ratio()` are both derived directly from this list: the gaps between blocks become `replace`/`delete`/`insert`, and the ratio is `2 * matched / (len(a) + len(b))`.

`find_longest_match` itself relies on `b2j`, an index built once per `b` that maps each element to the list of positions where it occurs in `b`. It walks `a` one element at a time, keeping `j2len[j]`, the length of the match ending at `a[i-1]` and `b[j]`. For each occurrence `j` of `a[i]` in `b`, the new length is `j2len[j-1] + 1`. The best is only replaced on a strictly longer match, so ties go to the block starting earliest in `a`, then earliest in `b`.

This greedy "longest block first" choice is why the result is not a minimal edit script. An early long match can rule out a set of shorter matches that would have covered more elements in total. The trade is deliberate: the output tends to line up the way a person would read the change.

**Junk** (the `isjunk` function you pass in) works by removing elements from `b2j`. This has two effects:

- **No match can be seeded on junk.** The main loop only ever sees non-junk positions, so the longest block is chosen among junk-free runs.
- **Junk can still end up inside a block.** After the best junk-free block is found, it is extended first over adjacent matching non-junk elements, then over adjacent matching junk elements on both sides.

So junk does not get excluded from the output; it just cannot be the reason two regions are aligned. In the docstring example with blanks as junk, `" abcd"` vs `"abcd abcd"` matches the leftmost `abcd` instead of latching onto the `" abcd"` at the end. A region containing only junk in common can still produce a block, because the empty "best" match gets extended over matching junk. Note that junk is determined only from `b`, so the two sequences are not treated symmetrically.

**Autojunk** is the same mechanism applied automatically. When `b` has at least 200 elements, any non-junk element that occurs more than `len(b) // 100 + 1` times is put in `bpopular` and deleted from `b2j`. It exists for speed: elements such as blank lines or `return NULL;` would otherwise make the inner loop visit hundreds of positions per element of `a`.

The difference from real junk shows in the extension step. Popular elements are not in `bjunk`, so they are picked up by the first (non-junk) extension loop and can be absorbed into a block that was seeded by something rarer. What they cannot do is seed a block themselves.

That has visible consequences for the result:

- **Missed matches.** A region whose common elements are all popular produces no block at all, so it shows up as a `replace` even where the two sides are identical.
- **Low ratios on low-alphabet input.** Comparing long strings character by character (for example DNA, or any text over 200 characters where most characters exceed the 1% threshold) can leave almost nothing in `b2j`, and `ratio()` comes out far lower than the true similarity.
- **Sudden change at 200 elements.** The same pair of inputs can diff differently just above and below that length.

Passing `autojunk=False` turns this off, at the cost of the quadratic behaviour it was added to avoid. `unified_diff`, `context_diff` and `Differ` all construct their matchers without that argument, so line-level diffs from those helpers always have autojunk on.

`limit_denominator` works because the loop narrows the search to exactly two candidates, one on each side of the value, with a guarantee that no other fraction with an allowed denominator can lie between them. Rounding cannot do this, because it only considers one denominator.

**Why not just round.** `round(x * M) / M` gives the nearest fraction whose denominator is `M` (or a divisor of it), not the nearest among all denominators up to `M`. For π with `M = 10`, rounding gives 31/10, which is off by about 0.04, while 22/7 is off by about 0.001. You could round for every denominator from 1 to `M` and keep the best, but that is `M` iterations (a million by default). The loop is Euclid's algorithm, so it takes a number of steps proportional to the number of digits in the denominator, and it uses only exact integer arithmetic.

**What the loop computes.** Each pass takes `a = n//d` and replaces `(n, d)` with `(d, n - a*d)`, which is Euclid's algorithm on the numerator and denominator. The quotients `a` are the continued fraction terms of the value. `p0/q0` and `p1/q1` are the two most recent convergents, built by the standard recurrence: the new convergent is `(p0 + a*p1)/(q0 + a*q1)`. Convergents alternate between being below and above the value, and consecutive ones always satisfy `|p1*q0 - p0*q1| = 1`.

The loop stops as soon as the next convergent's denominator `q2` would exceed `max_denominator`. The early return for `self._denominator <= max_denominator` guarantees this happens before `d` reaches zero, since the last convergent is the value itself.

**The two candidates.** After the loop, `p1/q1` is the last convergent that fits. The full step by `a` would overshoot the limit, so the code takes the largest partial step that fits: `k = (max_denominator - q0)//q1`, giving the semiconvergent `(p0 + k*p1)/(q0 + k*q1)`. Because `k < a`, this fraction is on the same side of the value as `p0/q0`, which is the opposite side from `p1/q1`. So the value is bracketed by the two candidates.

**Why nothing else can beat them.** The two candidates also satisfy the "determinant is ±1" property. For such a pair, any fraction strictly between them has a denominator at least the sum of their denominators. Here that sum is `q0 + (k+1)*q1`, which exceeds `max_denominator` by the choice of `k`. So no allowed fraction lies strictly between the candidates, and since the value itself is between them, the nearest allowed fraction must be one of the two.

**The final comparison.** The gap between the candidates is `1/(q1*(q0+k*q1))`. The loop maintains the invariant that `d` equals `|self._numerator*q1 - p1*self._denominator|`, so the distance from `p1/q1` to the value is `d/(q1*self._denominator)`. `p1/q1` wins when its distance is at most half the gap, which rearranges to the integer test `2*d*(q0+k*q1) <= self._denominator`. The `<=` sends ties to `p1/q1`, the candidate with the smaller denominator.

**Docstring example.** For 3.141592653589793 the convergents are 3/1, 22/7, 333/106, and so on.

- **Limit 10:** the loop stops with `p0/q0 = 3/1` and `p1/q1 = 22/7`. Then `k = 1`, so the candidates are 22/7 and 25/8, and 22/7 is closer.
- **Limit 100:** the loop stops at the same place, but `k = 14`. The semiconvergent is 311/99, which is closer than 22/7, so it wins.

**`firstweekday` and `monthdayscalendar`**

`firstweekday` only changes which weekday sits in column 0 of each row. The day numbers themselves are the same; what moves is the zero padding:

- **Leading zeros:** there are `(day1 - firstweekday) % 7` of them, where `day1` is the weekday of the 1st.
- **Trailing zeros:** enough to fill out the last week.
- **Row count:** because the padding shifts, the same month can come out with a different number of weeks (4 to 6). February 2021 starts on a Monday, so it is 4 rows with `firstweekday=0` but 5 rows with `firstweekday=6`.

The `Calendar` class does not validate the value; it just reduces it mod 7 when read. Only the module-level `setfirstweekday()` raises `IllegalWeekdayError`.

**`itermonthdates` at the edges of the year range**

Yes, there is a surprise: it can raise `ValueError` for a month that is itself perfectly valid. It builds a `datetime.date` for every day of the complete weeks, including the padding days from the neighbouring months. At the two ends of the range those padding days do not exist as `date` objects:

- **January of year 1:** 1 January 0001 is a Monday. With the default `firstweekday=0` there is no leading padding and it works. With any other `firstweekday`, the first padding day is in December of year 0 and the first `next()` raises.
- **December 9999:** 31 December 9999 is a Friday. With the default `firstweekday=0`, it yields every valid date and then raises at the very end when it reaches 1 January 10000. With `firstweekday=5` (Saturday) there is no trailing padding and it completes.

So whether these months work depends on `firstweekday`, and because it is a generator the error appears mid-iteration rather than at the call. `monthdatescalendar` and `yeardatescalendar` inherit the same failure, so `Calendar().yeardatescalendar(9999)` fails with the defaults.

The tuple-based `itermonthdays3` and `itermonthdays4` exist to avoid this, and `itermonthdays` is also unaffected. They even work for years outside 1..9999, because `weekday()` maps such years onto an equivalent year in the 400-year cycle instead of raising.

`budget.py` now takes an optional month: `python3 budget.py 2026-09` counts only September's transactions, and with no argument it prints exactly what it did before. I ran it both ways against your data:

| Envelope | No month (all transactions) | `2026-09` |
|---|---|---|
| groceries | 174.60 | 371.55 |
| fuel | 22.85 | 124.75 |
| eating out | 45.75 | 84.25 |
| household | 54.61 | 101.60 |

- **Bad input:** a month that doesn't parse (`sept`, `2026-13`) or an extra argument prints a short message to stderr and exits with status 2.
- **Empty month:** a month with no transactions (e.g. `2026-10`) shows every envelope at its full allocation rather than an error.
